## The idea

History matters when what happens now changes the odds of what happens next. Choose a QWERTY keyboard, a railway gauge or a video format, and every adopter makes the next adopter more likely to choose the same. The Polya process captures this with an urn: draw a ball, then return it together with another ball of the same colour. Each draw reinforces itself.

The result is *path dependence*. Early draws, which are pure chance, shift the urn's composition, and later draws can only partly undo them. Run the process many times and the long-run share of white balls settles down in every run, but at a different value each time, and every value between 0 and 1 is equally likely. Page also notes a subtler property: the probability of any sequence depends only on how many of each colour it contains, not on their order. The outcome distribution is path dependent; the probability of reaching it is not.

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Setup.** An urn starts with one white and one gray ball. Each period a ball is drawn at random, and it is returned along with one more ball of the same colour. The outcome is the colour drawn.

**Equation.** After $t$ draws with $w_t$ white draws, the urn holds $t + 2$ balls, $w_t + 1$ of them white, so

$$
\Pr(\text{white at } t + 1) = \frac{w_t + 1}{t + 2} .
$$

**Results.**

- The share of white balls converges in every run, but its limit is random and uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$. (Starting from $a$ white and $b$ gray balls, the limit has a Beta$(a, b)$ distribution.)
- Any sequence with $w$ white draws out of $t$ has probability $\dfrac{w!\,(t - w)!}{(t+1)!}$, whatever the order.
:::

## Interactive model

Each line is one urn followed for the chosen number of draws. The lines start out jagged, then flatten at a value fixed mostly by the first few draws. The histogram shows the final white share of 3,000 urns: with one ball of each colour to start, it is flat. Change the starting balls to see the limit concentrate.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, C, fmt, pct} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof white0 = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Starting white balls"})
viewof gray0 = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Starting gray balls"})
viewof draws = Inputs.range([50, 2000], {value: 500, step: 50, label: "Draws"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 28, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
polya = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const run = (record) => {
    let w = white0, g = gray0;
    const path = record ? [{t: 0, share: w / (w + g)}] : null;
    for (let t = 1; t <= draws; t++) {
      if (r() < w / (w + g)) w++; else g++;
      if (record && (t % 5 === 0 || t < 50)) path.push({t, share: w / (w + g)});
    }
    return record ? path : w / (w + g);
  };
  const paths = range(12).flatMap(k => run(true).map(d => ({...d, k})));
  const finals = range(3000).map(() => run(false));
  const after20 = range(400).map(() => { let w = white0, g = gray0; for (let t = 0; t < 20; t++) { if (r() < w / (w + g)) w++; else g++; } const s20 = w / (w + g); for (let t = 20; t < draws; t++) { if (r() < w / (w + g)) w++; else g++; } return {s20, sEnd: w / (w + g)}; });
  const corr = d3.mean(after20, d => d.s20 * d.sEnd) - d3.mean(after20, d => d.s20) * d3.mean(after20, d => d.sEnd);
  const r20 = corr / (d3.deviation(after20, d => d.s20) * d3.deviation(after20, d => d.sEnd));
  return {paths, finals, r20};
}
```


## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Polya process: self-reinforcing urns settle at random limits.
white0 <- 1
gray0 <- 1
draws <- 500
set.seed(28)

polya <- function() {
  w <- white0
  g <- gray0
  share <- numeric(draws)
  for (t in 1:draws) {
    if (runif(1) < w / (w + g)) w <- w + 1 else g <- g + 1
    share[t] <- w / (w + g)
  }
  share
}
paths <- replicate(12, polya())
finals <- replicate(3000, tail(polya(), 1))
cat("Final shares of 3000 urns by decile (uniform if flat):\n")
print(round(quantile(finals, seq(0, 1, 0.1)), 2))
cat(sprintf(
  "Correlation of share after 20 draws with final share: %.2f\n",
  cor(paths[20, ], paths[draws, ])
))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(paths,
  type = "l", lty = 1, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Draws",
  ylab = "Share white", col = hcl.colors(12)
)
hist(finals,
  breaks = 20, col = "#148a91", border = "white", main = "",
  xlab = "Final share white"
)
```

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- Self-reinforcing choices make outcomes path dependent: early random events determine where the process settles.
- In the classic urn, every long-run share is equally likely, so the eventual outcome is unpredictable in advance.
- The probability of a final composition does not depend on the order of the draws that produced it.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Explain.** Technology lock-in (QWERTY, VHS, railway gauges), the persistence of early market leaders, and why history matters for which cities grow.
- **Reason.** Distinguish path dependence from tipping points: here every step matters a little, rather than one moment mattering a lot.
- **Act.** Early interventions, when the urn holds few balls, have far more leverage than late ones.
:::

- [Balancing Process](balancing-process.qmd): the opposite rule, which pulls every urn back to 50–50.
